clue.text: Boatman's head abroad to retire

parts.note: the bow is the front, or head, of a boat
someone abroad is out of the country, away from home

explanation.surface: The setter, who calls himself Boatman, has his chief planning to quit and live overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: Boatman is the setter's own pseudonym, so the surface invites you to think of a person; the wordplay wants the front of an actual boat.
explanation.definitionFit: To bow out is an idiom for withdrawing gracefully from a job or activity, which is what retiring means.

clue.text: Type of sink of which fables might be spun on completion of refit

indicators.note: a yarn that is spun is twisted into a new form, so the letters get rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the completion of a word is where it ends, so only its final letter is wanted

parts.note: the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone renovating a kitchen picks a sink that comes with a story or two told about it.
explanation.walkthrough: To spin a yarn is to tell a tale, so 'fables might be spun' reads naturally as storytelling. A Belfast sink is a deep, square, white ceramic sink with an overflow, popular in farmhouse-style kitchens.
explanation.definitionFit: Belfast is the name given to a particular style of deep ceramic kitchen basin, named after the city in Northern Ireland.

clue.text: Put together with kitchen appliance

parts.note: W is the standard abbreviation for with
an oven is a kitchen appliance for baking and roasting

explanation.surface: Flat-pack instructions: assemble this unit along with the cooker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put together' sounds like assembling furniture, but it is the definition, in the past participle form.
explanation.definitionFit: Threads that have been woven are interlaced to form one fabric, so they have been combined into a single whole.

clue.text: Stripped out one slum dwelling, rented unfinished for free

indicators.note: something left unfinished lacks its end, so the last letter goes
stripping peels away the outside, leaving only the inner letters

parts.note: the inside of this three-letter word
the inside of this three-letter word
a shack is a crude hut, the kind found in a shanty town
a property that is rented out has been let

explanation.surface: A poor tenant has been cleaned out of a slum flat and given a half-finished lease for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stripped' governs both 'out' and 'one', leaving the middle letter of each; 'free' at the end looks like 'for free', but it is the definition, a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To unshackle is to remove chains or restraints from someone, releasing them, so it works as a synonym of the verb.

clue.text: Where to write in crossword grid after answer is set down

definitions.note: the definition is a passive phrase; the answer is the active verb with the same sense of coming to rest

indicators.note: one piece coming after another means it follows it in the reading order

parts.note: A is the standard abbreviation for answer

parts.words: Where to write in crossword grid
parts.note: lights are the runs of white squares in a crossword where the letters go

explanation.surface: Instructions to the solver: once the answer is fixed, here is where to fill it in.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about the very act of solving; 'lights' is crossword jargon for the answer spaces in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird or passenger that alights comes down and settles on a perch or platform, landing after a journey.

clue.text: Decoration around worksurfaces: it's fiddly!

indicators.note: to go around something is to enclose it on both sides

parts.note: a medal or honour is an award
read as 'work surfaces': the surfaces of the word 'work' are its outer letters

explanation.surface: A kitchen fitter grumbles that the trim around the counters is tricky to install.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worksurfaces' looks like kitchen counters; split it as 'work surfaces' and the outside letters of 'work' are what is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Something awkward is hard to handle or do, requiring care and dexterity, which is how a fiddly task feels.

clue.text: Suggest island unit of length to satisfy catering needs

parts.note: I is the standard abbreviation for island
M is the symbol for metre
to ply someone is to keep supplying them with food or drink

explanation.surface: A caterer proposes shipping supplies by the metre to an island to meet demand.
explanation.walkthrough: Ply here is the verb of 'plied with drink', keeping guests supplied.
explanation.definitionFit: To imply something is to hint at it without stating it outright, which is one sense of the verb suggest.

clue.text: Camouflage guide, say as a shrub

indicators.note: to say something is to speak it, so the sound matters, not the spelling

parts.note: to camouflage is to hide; a Ranger is a senior member of the Girl Guides

explanation.surface: A scout leader is told to disguise himself as a bush.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain, Rangers are the oldest section of Girlguiding, so a guide can be a ranger. 'Say' looks like 'for example' but is asking for the sound.
explanation.definitionFit: The hydrangea is a flowering garden bush with large round heads of blue, pink or white blossom.

clue.text: Balance plates …

definitions.meaning: second meaning: the overlapping protective plates on a fish or reptile

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on into the next clue, suggesting a juggler keeping plates balanced; here the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A weighing device with two pans is a balance, and the hard overlapping flakes covering a fish are its protective plating.

clue.text: … perhaps spinning on supports a short time before it tips up

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece that supports another sits underneath it
coming before means placed earlier in the reading order

parts.note: a mo is a moment, as in 'wait a mo'

indicators.note: in a down clue, tipping something up turns it upside down so it reads bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: the plates spin on their poles briefly before toppling over.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links to the plate-spinning scene of the previous clue. 'Perhaps' marks spinning as just one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Spinning is one kind of movement, so it is an example of the broader noun for something changing position.

clue.text: The herd passes its days by the sound of the clock

parts.note: to pass one's days somewhere is to live there
tick-tock is the noise a clock makes

explanation.surface: Cattle spend their days measured by the ticking of a farmhouse clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The herd' looks like part of the scene but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Farm animals kept for meat, milk or wool are collectively called livestock, so a herd is an example.

clue.text: Raised supports for lids of pans on display in armoire

indicators.note: a lid sits on top, so each word gives up only its topmost, first letter

parts.note: the opening letter of each of these five words

explanation.surface: Stands to show off saucepan lids inside a wardrobe-style cupboard.
explanation.walkthrough: In a kitchen-themed puzzle, 'lids of pans' is a natural phrase; here 'lids' means initial letters. An armoire is a tall cupboard or wardrobe.
explanation.definitionFit: Podia is the plural of podium, an elevated platform on which a speaker or winner stands.

clue.text: Not breathing, leap, neatly catching this

indicators.note: to catch something is to hold it within, so the letters lie inside the phrase

parts.note: runs across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A diver jumps cleanly and holds their breath on the way down.
explanation.walkthrough: APNEA is the American spelling of apnoea.
explanation.definitionFit: Apnea is the medical term for a temporary suspension of respiration, as in sleep apnea.

clue.text: Foolish to keep every other one of my scraps, no matter what

indicators.note: keeping something means holding it inside

parts.note: inane means silly or senseless

indicators.note: every other one means alternate letters, skipping one each time

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: A hoarder, daft enough to hang on to half of their leftovers whatever happens.
explanation.walkthrough: Start from the second letter of 'my scraps' to get the even letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are idioms meaning regardless of circumstances, used to say something holds whatever else is true.

clue.text: Set of modifications to kitchen

indicators.note: making modifications changes the form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A list of changes planned for a kitchen refit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set' looks like a noun, a set of changes; it is the verb, as a jelly or sauce sets.
explanation.definitionFit: When a liquid sets it becomes firm or stiff, so it grows more viscous, the cooking sense of the verb.

clue.text: Loneliness is over: passionate about love

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it

parts.note: taken as written
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over
Latin temperaments are stereotypically fiery and passionate
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O

explanation.surface: Someone declares their lonely days are finished, now that they are mad about love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is over' reads as 'has ended', but it splits into two pieces. Latin as 'passionate' is the cliché of the Latin lover.
explanation.definitionFit: Isolation is the state of being cut off from other people, which brings the feeling of being alone.

clue.text: Contrarily, say 'a potty break'

indicators.note: acting contrarily means going the opposite way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: e.g. means 'for example', as does say
taken as written
potty is British slang for crazy

explanation.surface: A cheeky euphemism for stopping to use the toilet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A potty break' sounds like a toddler's toilet stop; 'break' is the definition, a verb, and 'potty' means crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: To damage something is to harm or impair it, one everyday sense of the verb break.

clue.text: Something of a charmer, Ma identified as a nymph

indicators.note: something of a thing is a part of it, so the letters lie within

parts.note: runs from the end of the first word through to the middle of the third

explanation.surface: Mother has been spotted as a seductive water spirit, quite the enchantress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Something of a charmer' reads as a description of Ma, but the first two words point at the run of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A mermaiden is an old poetic word for a mermaid, a sea creature from folklore much like a water sprite.

clue.text: Reports of can opener, extra small

definitions.note: a journalist covers a story, so 'reports of' stands for the verb with its object to follow

indicators.note: an opener is what starts things off, so the first letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of the word
left over means extra, surplus to need
S is the standard abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: Product reviews of a tin opener in an extra-small size.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can opener' is a kitchen gadget, but here 'opener' takes the first letter of 'can'.
explanation.definitionFit: To cover a news event is the journalistic term for writing about it, giving an account to readers.

clue.text: Cross is vandalised and cut

indicators.note: something vandalised has been smashed up and is no longer in its proper form

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A memorial cross has been defaced and hacked about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like an angry adjective or a monument; it is simply letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To scissor something is to snip it with shears, so as a verb it means to slice or trim.

clue.text: Alongside breakfast bar: cocktail function to be rescheduled

indicators.note: rescheduling moves things into a new order
bar here means except, so the following pieces are left out

parts.note: taken as written
read as 'cock tail': the tail, or last letter, of 'cock'
F is the mathematician's abbreviation for function, as in f(x)

explanation.surface: Next to the breakfast counter, a drinks party has had to change its date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breakfast bar' is a kitchen counter, but 'bar' means 'except'; 'cocktail' splits into 'cock tail'.
explanation.definitionFit: Walking abreast means side by side in a line, each person level with the next, so it means beside.

clue.text: Counter with one incomplete support half-used

indicators.note: incomplete means missing its end, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: a means one, as in 'a dozen'
to back someone is to support them

indicators.note: only half survives, so the back half of the word is removed

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A kitchen counter with one leg short, only partly put to use.
explanation.walkthrough: In a kitchen puzzle 'counter' suggests a worktop; it is a thing that counts.
explanation.definitionFit: An abacus is a frame of sliding beads used for arithmetic, an early calculating device that tallies numbers.

clue.text: Kitchen appliance rotates while cooking

indicators.note: cooking transforms the ingredients, and the letters are likewise transformed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A gadget that turns round as it heats food, like a rotisserie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooking' slang for something being cooked up or altered is a common signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A toaster is a small electrical device for browning slices of bread, found on most kitchen counters.

clue.text: Before music begins, stop man from talking. See you listened to soft rock

indicators.note: placed before means earlier in the reading order
to stop one thing from another is to keep it out, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: taken as written
a king is a chess man

indicators.note: what is listened to is heard, so the sound of the words is wanted rather than their spelling

parts.note: the letters C and U spoken aloud, as in text-speak

indicators.note: where a word begins is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A parent hushes someone before a concert starts, then leaves for a rock gig.
explanation.walkthrough: The sentence order is shuffled: the first phrase tells you the music letter comes last. Chess pieces are called men, so 'man' can be the king.
explanation.definitionFit: Talc is the softest mineral on the hardness scale, and talcum is another name for that stone.

clue.text: American Right are rebuked, including number one web users

indicators.note: including something means taking it in, so one piece holds another

parts.note: A is the standard abbreviation for American
R is the standard abbreviation for right
an are is a metric unit of area, abbreviated A
chid is an old past tense of chide, to scold
N is the abbreviation for number
a means one, as in 'a dozen'

explanation.surface: US conservatives get a telling-off, including the top internet users.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Web users' looks like people online; it is the spiders. 'Number one' is a false phrase: the two words give separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Arachnida is the zoological class containing spiders, which spin silk webs to trap prey.

clue.text: Composer discovered tempo initially to be off

definitions.note: the answer is an imperative, 'go away', while the definition is the infinitive

parts.note: the inner letters of Chopin, the Polish composer

indicators.note: dis-covered means with the cover taken off, leaving only the inside
initially means at the start, so the first letter

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A composer realised the tempo was wrong from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discovered' reads as 'found out'; split it as 'dis-covered', uncovered. Hop it is British slang for 'go away'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hop it is a slangy British command telling someone to leave at once, the same as clear off.

clue.text: One endless tease with section misplaced. Boatman can be thus

parts.note: a means one, as in 'a dozen'

indicators.note: something misplaced is put in the wrong position, so the order changes
without an end means the last letter is removed

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A setter jokes that his own clues can leave him confused.
explanation.walkthrough: Boatman is the setter's name, so he can be on the water or bewildered; the 'section' moved is one letter of the clipped word.
explanation.definitionFit: A sailor is literally out on the ocean, and the idiom also means confused, both fitting a setter called Boatman.

clue.text: Cooker broke

definitions.meaning: second meaning: past tense of stave, to smash a hole in

explanation.walkthrough: Read together it sounds like a broken oven; the past tense of 'stave' is the less familiar second meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A kitchen range used for heating pans is one sense, and the past tense of stave, to puncture or smash, is the other.

clue.text: Primate (Catholic) with gas hob?

parts.note: C is the standard abbreviation for Catholic
H is the chemical symbol for hydrogen, a gas
a hob is a hobgoblin, a mischievous sprite

explanation.surface: An archbishop, the senior cleric of his church, cooking on a gas ring.
explanation.walkthrough: A Primate is the senior archbishop of a country, which the bracketed Catholic encourages; 'gas hob' is a cooker, but split, gas and hob each give a piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A chimpanzee is an ape, and apes belong to the mammal order that includes monkeys and humans.

clue.text: Canvasses of Islay and Jura, for example, and Forth

parts.words: of Islay and Jura, for example
parts.note: the Sound of Islay and the Sound of Jura are sea channels off western Scotland
to go forth is to go out

explanation.surface: A tour of Scottish waters: two Hebridean islands and the Firth of Forth.
explanation.walkthrough: Islay and Jura are islands of the Inner Hebrides; a sound is a narrow sea strait. 'Forth' looks like the Scottish estuary but is the adverb.
explanation.definitionFit: To sound someone out is to probe their opinion discreetly, just as canvassing asks people their views.

clue.text: Tap made of metal put back in rear-facing part of house

indicators.note: putting something back sends it the opposite way
facing the rear means looking backwards, so the letters run in the reverse order
one thing in another sits inside it

parts.note: a room is a part of a house
tin is a metal

explanation.surface: A plumber's note: the metal tap belongs in the back kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tap' looks like a plumbing fitting, especially with 'metal' beside it; it means eavesdropping on a phone line.
explanation.definitionFit: To tap a phone is to listen in secretly, which is a form of keeping watch on someone's calls, surveillance.

clue.text: Mobilise, or Reform gain, re-enabled to move forward

indicators.note: to reform something is to give it a new shape

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, the first two letters of the next word

explanation.surface: A political call to action: rally the troops or else regain lost ground under Reform and press ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: Reform UK is a British political party, which makes 'Reform gain' look like an election result. The fodder ends partway through 're-enabled'.
explanation.definitionFit: A vehicle with its transmission engaged is ready to drive, as opposed to being in neutral, idling.
